Area.evidence_source: [/page/16/Text/14] The majority of prisoners stated that their suicide attempts were serious acts intended to end their lives, and most were certain that their chosen method would be lethal. Despite this a large number of prisoners described their acts as impulsive thinking about and planning their future action for only a very short time (typically less than three hours). Similarly, very few prisoners took any precautions against discovery, wrote a suicide note, made any plans or arrangements for death or thought about the timing of the act. This is in contrast to the way that the suicidal process is normally conceptualised in the community. Usually, both researchers and clinicians assume that the longer a participant or patient has been thinking about, and planning, their suicide, the more likely they 'really' meant to die (Hawton & Catalan, 1987). Evidence of this way of thinking comes, for example, from the Suicide Intent Scale (Beck et al., 1974), where suicide attempters score more highly the more time they have devoted to thinking about, or planning, the act. The impulsive nature of [/page/17/Text/2] many of the acts by cases in this study, however, indicates that this conceptualisation may not be as valid in prisons as in the general population, because impulsivity does not seem to be inversely associated with the seriousness of intent to die. [/page/17/Text/3] One reason for this may be that characteristics of the prison environment and/or prisoners distort or alter many of the traditional factors that are associated with being 'serious' about dying by suicide.
